title: What happens to the arcs when the lengths do not fit?
description: A triangle is tried with sides of three, four and eight centimetres, then with two, three and six, and in both cases the arcs from the ends of the base fall short of each other. Keeko doubts the result and wants to draw longer arcs to make them meet.
teaching_notes: One idea: two arcs meet only if the two shorter lengths together reach past the longest side. Watch for children who think longer arcs will eventually cross, when each arc keeps the same radius however long it is drawn.

source: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm.
video_script.why: The child has built triangles from three lengths every time and now meets lengths for which the arcs never cross.
video_script.substitution: The base is the longest side and the two arcs have the two shorter lengths as their radii.
video_script.anchor: A base with an arc from each end that do not meet
video_script.wrong_answer: draw longer arcs to make them meet
video_script.wrong_move: A child sees the arcs fall short of each other and draws them longer, hoping they will cross, though each arc keeps the same radius however long it is drawn.
video_script.payoff_line: No triangle can be built for either set, because the arcs never meet.

final_answer.spoken: no triangle can be built for three, four and eight, or for two, three and six

never_show: the words no triangle before the answer beat
maths_rules: base AB = 8 cm; arc from A reaches 3 cm along AB; arc from B reaches 4 cm along BA
3 + 4 = 7, and 7 < 8, so a gap of 1 cm is left and the arcs do not meet
base 6 cm; arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm reach 2 + 3 = 5, and 5 < 6, so a gap of 1 cm is left
in both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 < 8 and 2 + 3 < 6
video_script.design: One idea: the arcs meet only if the two shorter lengths together reach past the longest side. One base, two short arcs and a gap between them; Keeko's doubt closes the video.
